title: A Sun-Powered Air Engine
question: How does moving air carry heat from the tropics toward the poles?
hook: The air around you is part of a planet-sized engine that runs on sunlight and dumps its heat into space.
idea: Warm air rises, travels poleward, cools and sinks in great loops, moving heat from the tropics toward the poles and out to space.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of the Hadley cell's loop in order.
items: Moist air is warmed at the equator and rises
The air moves poleward high up
It cools and sinks near the 30th parallel
It flows back toward the equator along the surface
beats.explain: Warmed air rises at the equator, travels poleward, cools and descends near 30°, then returns along the surface to replace the air that rose.

beats.prompt: Air sinks near 30° latitude and builds an area of high pressure. What weather would you expect there?

choices.label: Light winds, sunny skies, little rain
Heavy daily thunderstorms
choices.feedback: Tempting for a warm region, but this zone typically has little precipitation.

choices.label: Constant strong gales
choices.feedback: Winds spread apart here, and they are typically light.

beats.explain: The horse latitudes, at about 30° to 35°, are a high-pressure area with light winds, sunny skies and little precipitation.

beats.prompt: Match each part of the circulation to its description.
pairs: Surface easterlies of the Hadley cell
Surface winds of the polar cell
beats.explain: Each cell has a place where air rises and a surface wind that flows back, deflected by the Coriolis effect.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Air rising at the equator moves poleward high up
Coriolis acceleration turns that upper air toward the east
Near the ground, air returning to the equator turns west
So the surface trade winds blow from the west
beats.explain: Air turned toward the west is a wind from the east: the trade winds are easterlies.
